title: How do generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools and large language models (LLMs) influence language learners’ critical thinking in EFL education? A systematic review
extended_summary:
This paper addresses a timely question in education: whether generative AI tools and large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT support or undermine critical thinking in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) education. The authors note that prior work has focused mainly on technical benefits like grammar correction, vocabulary development, and writing support, while giving less attention to higher-order thinking. To address this gap, they conduct a systematic review focused specifically on critical thinking in EFL contexts.

Using the PRISMA framework, the authors searched Web of Science, Scopus, ProQuest, ERIC, and Google Scholar for studies published from 2022 to February 2025. After screening 3,243 records plus 4 additional sources, they included 15 studies. The review synthesizes evidence on the dual nature of generative AI and LLMs, the research methods used, the main thematic focuses, the theories and models applied, and the limitations and future directions in this research area. The reviewed studies concern EFL learners and teachers, with contexts including classroom teaching and language learning activities such as writing, speaking, argumentation, and literature learning.

The main conclusion is that generative AI and LLMs have both promise and risk for critical thinking in EFL education. Ten of the 15 studies (66.67%) reported positive effects, including improved argumentative writing and speaking, stronger analytical reasoning, better evaluation and problem-solving, increased engagement and confidence, and support for self-directed learning. At the same time, five studies (33.33%) warned that overreliance on AI could reduce analytical depth, creativity, autonomy, and independent reasoning. The authors conclude that AI can nurture critical thinking when used with guidance, critical evaluation, and pedagogical structure, but may hinder it when learners passively accept AI-generated content.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generative AI tools and large language model-powered applications used in EFL education, including chatbots and writing/speaking support systems, treated at the category level across multiple heterogeneous tools.
identified_tools.use_case: Systematic review of 15 empirical studies examining how generative AI/LLM tools influence critical thinking in English as a Foreign Language education.

findings.finding_summary: Across 15 reviewed studies in EFL contexts, 66.67% of studies reported a positive role of generative AI/LLMs in fostering critical thinking, while 33.33% reported negative effects. Positive findings included improvements in argumentative speaking, writing quality, analytical thinking, reasoning, evaluation, decision-making, problem-solving, creativity, collaboration, engagement, motivation, confidence, and self-directed learning; negative findings centered on overreliance, passive thinking, reduced analytical depth, weaker autonomy, and reduced creativity.
findings.measure: Critical thinking and related higher-order skills in EFL learning tasks across included studies

findings.finding_summary: The review reports that generative AI tools supported EFL literacy-related outcomes such as writing quality, argument structure, logic flow, evidence evaluation, and speech/script writing in multiple included studies. Examples summarized in the review include AI-supported writing tasks, argumentative speaking performance, and revised drafts showing changes in claims, warrants, and grounds, though no pooled effect size was reported.
findings.measure: EFL writing quality, argumentative speaking, speech/script writing, and revision features

findings.finding_summary: Five of the 15 reviewed studies cautioned that generative AI use may hinder critical thinking by encouraging reliance on AI-generated content instead of deep analysis. Reported risks included passive thinking, decline in analytical depth, reduced creativity, and impeded development of autonomous analytical skills.
findings.measure: Critical thinking depth, autonomy, creativity, and independent analysis

quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review, but it is not a meta-analysis and synthesizes mostly qualitative, mixed-methods, and heterogeneous primary studies without pooled effect estimates. The evidence base is informative but methodologically varied.
impact_tier_rationale: The review finds mixed impact overall: most included studies were positive, but a substantial minority reported harms or risks, and no pooled effect sizes were reported. Impact is therefore promising but unclear in magnitude.
